knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative

question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the $2 x^{2}$ that's outside the square root isn't quite the derivative of $(-1-{x}^{3}).$ But the derivative is $- 3 x^{2},$ so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution

$$
u=-1-{x}^{3}.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =- 3 x^{2}\,⟹\,(- \frac{2}{3})\text{d}u=2 x^{2}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2 x^{2}\sqrt{-1-{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{-1-{x}^{3}}\cdot 2 x^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ & =\int \sqrt{u}\cdot (- \frac{2}{3})\text{d}u \\ & =- \frac{2}{3}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}- \frac{2}{3}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =(- \frac{2}{3})\cdot \frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\ & =(- \frac{2}{3})\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {u}^{3/2}+C \\ & =- \frac{4}{9}{u}^{3/2}+C \\ & =- \frac{4}{9}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}+C \\ & =- \frac{4}{9}\sqrt{(-1-{x}^{3})^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
